As the No. 19 Ole Miss football team was upset by the unranked Oklahoma Sooners on Sunday afternoon, 24-17, the conversation around the game was about how the contest was moved from Saturday. While Oklahoma head coach Brent Venables called it ‘insensitive’ to move the Ole Miss football matchup because of the fans, Pete Golding has his own thoughts on the situation. The reason for the change was that the Rebels and other college football teams had their flight plans disrupted after a nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) . There was no doubt transgressions on the side of the Sooners, as the program questioned if the Rebels exhausted every measure to get their team in Norman, Oklahoma, on time. With the game moved to Sunday, Golding said after the loss that he promised that “nobody was more frustrated than our team.” Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) “I promise you, nobody was more frustrated than our team that got to a facility at 7:45 on Friday morning. And we’re sitting on buses for three hours and sitting under a stadium and got called back and in meeting rooms, and we’re holding them,” Golding said, via Joe Mussato. “There was nobody more frustrated; I can assure you they didn’t want to wait another day. You know, everybody wanted to exhaust everything that we could to get here Friday night. You know, they called us and told us we weren’t able to do that.” “I promise you, nobody was more frustrated than our team.” Ole Miss coach Pete Golding on the tension regarding the schedule change: pic.twitter.com/PN3BQbpLtv — Joe Mussatto (@joe_mussatto) November 15, 2026 Ole Miss football’s Pete Golding continues on moving the game to Sunday Golding continued about the Ole Miss football program having to move the game, with him saying that it reminded him of when COVID-19 halted the sports world and how teams had to work around it. “We didn’t get to decide this, we didn’t get to choose this, but it is what it is…Let’s go show up. top.description: Troy Taormina-Imagn Images Texans’ Kamari Lassiter is completely dumbfounded at penalty that cost him crucial INT appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . The Houston Texans fought a close contest against the Cleveland Browns. It seemed as if Houston would leave this game with a victory. Kamari Lassiter came up with what looked like quite the interception. This was until the yellow flag hit the field. Lassiter was flagged for unnecessary roughness on the play. He did make contact with the receiver as he made an attempt to disrupt the pass, leading to the flag. After the game, the Texans star expressed his issues with the call. “It’s very frustrating, I mean, because as a player, it leaves you with a lot of indecision. We play a violent sport, I don’t think that, I don’t know, I’m confused,” Lassiter said, via KPRC2 reporter Aaron Wilson. Houston failed to score at all as they dropped their sixth game of the season on Sunday. This is certainly a brutal loss for Houston to process. They now sit at 3-6 with fading playoff hopes. top.title: 'Couldn't get worse': Klopp calls for change in FIFA leadership
top.description: Germany coach Jurgen Klopp has called for a change in FIFA leadership. (Pedja Milosavljevic) Germany coach Jurgen Klopp called on Sunday for an end to Gianni Infantino's time as FIFA president, saying he "did not think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter." Speaking in Berlin ahead of Monday's Nations League clash with the Netherlands, Klopp said the next candidate for football's global governing body should have the game's interests at heart. "I've been following football for many years. There are people who are much more knowledgeable about this than I am. But I think most people now agree a change would make a lot of sense," Klopp said. "I didn't think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that." President of FIFA from 1998, Blatter resigned in disgrace in 2015 amid corruption allegations, including accusations he had sought to buy votes for his presidency. Charges were brought against Blatter who was eventually cleared in two trials, but was banned from football by FIFA's ethics committee. Klopp added: "Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job." Swiss Infantino succeeded Blatter as FIFA president in 2016 and has come under heavy criticism for a series of decisions and proposals, including his plan to sell off part of the commercial rights of the World Cup and creating a 'Peace Prize' award for US President Donald Trump. "There are people who truly care about the future of football -- people who aren't driven by financial interests," said Klopp. "If someone like that were to step up -- if someone like that were to become president -- I think that would be a significant improvement." "There are surely people who care deeply about the future of football and have no financial interests in it." The next election for FIFA president takes place in March 2027. Only former Swiss footballer Ramon Vega and Japan's Kozo Tashima have announced their intention to run against Infantino although Arsene Wenger has also been mentioned. Klopp did not discuss the other candidates, but said: "I've heard something about Arsene Wenger. Not sure if that's true or false, but he's a good man." dwi/td/pb

top.title: Rangers acquire struggling depth goalie Soderblom from Blackhawks
top.description: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The goalie depth chart in the New York Rangers organization received yet another minor reshuffling Sunday, when they acquired Arvid Soderblom from the Chicago Blackhawks in exchange for Spencer Martin . Soderblom will swap places with Martin on the Hartford Wolf Pack roster in the American Hockey League. The move nets the Rangers a goalie four years younger than Martin, and one who has 44 more games of NHL experience. The 27-year-old native of Sweden, struggled mightily for the woeful Blackhawks this season. In five games (four starts) for the Blackhawks, Soderblom was winless (0-3-1), with a 4.67 goals-against average and .842 save percentage in a backup role behind Spencer Knight. Chicago (5-13-2) has the second worst points percentage (.300) in the NHL. Soderblom played well in two starts for AHL Rockford after the Blackhawks sent him to the minors this past week. He won each game, allowed two goals total, and had a .957 save percentage. He will now share the net with 22-year-old goalie Callum Tung in Hartford. His acquisition gives the Rangers a more viable No. 3 goalie on the depth chart. New York had little faith in Martin, who’s 31 and didn’t exactly excel in the NHL last season when Igor Shesterkin landed on IR for a month with a lower-body injury in January. Soderblom played more than 30 games twice in the NHL, and owns a 3.65 GAA and .885 save percentage in 117 games over parts of six seasons with the Blackhawks. Rangers goalie shuffle continues with acquisition of Arvid Soderblom The trade occurred a few hours after the Rangers officially placed Shesterkin on season-ending injured reserve. Shesterkin sustained a severe knee injury Oct. 9 that requires surgery. The Rangers previously announced that the 30-year-old will miss the rest of the season, but up until Sunday, Shesterkin remained on long-term injured reserve. Now, he officially can’t play again until the 2027-28 season. After his injury, the Rangers relied heavily on 24-year-old rookie Dylan Garand because veteran backup Joonas Korpisalo was already out for a month due to a foot infection. Martin was recalled from Hartford to back up Garand, and then was replaced by veteran James Reimer, who played one game before the Rangers terminated his contract more than a week ago upon Korpisalo’s return. top.title: England topple Spain as Belgium smash Italy to reach Nations League quarters
top.description: Harry Kane celebrates sending England on their way to a famous win against Spain (Thomas COEX) England ended Spain's unbeaten run in competitive matches at 44 on Sunday, beating the world champions 3-2 on their own patch, while Belgium thumped Italy 4-1 to join France in the Nations League quarter-finals. Thomas Tuchel's team win Group A3, level on 15 points with Spain, after the hugely impressive win in Madrid in which La Roja were for long periods made to look a shadow of the team which won the World Cup. But the Three Lions ended up down to 10 men and hanging on by their finger nails before inflicting on Spain a first defeat in a competitive fixture since March 2023. Asked by ITV whether this was England's best performance of his reign as coach, Tuchel said: "Under the circumstances against who and where we played, yeah." "(We showed) what we are made of and what we can do," added Tuchel, saying his team were motivated by their third place at the World Cup. "We are always ready to push our limits. We had our best result in 60 years and we weren't happy with it. It's impressive what we did in the last two camps." Harry Kane put the away side deservedly ahead on the stroke of half time, netting from the penalty spot, his record-extending 93rd England goal. Ezri Konsa struck just after the break before Ben White gave England a barely-believable lead in the 57th minute when he latched onto Jude Bellingham's pass and finished between Unai Simon's legs. England needed that cushion. Moments later they found themselves a man down when Elliot Anderson hauled backed Lamine Yamal in the box, conceding a penalty and a red card. Mikel Oyarzabal slotted home the spot-kick with Spain's first shot on target to set up a grandstand finish and bring back memories of England's collapse against Argentina which cost them a place in the World Cup final. Those jitters intensified when Nico Williams slammed home Lamine Yamal's inch-perfect cross with 15 minutes remaining, but England just about held out under a Spanish onslaught. - Belgium rout Italy - Sitting third in Group A1 ahead of kick-off and needing a win to qualify for the last eight, Belgium had their backs up against the wall when Francesco Pio Esposito volleyed Italy ahead in the 11th minute. But Belgium blew Italy away in the following quarter of an hour, with Maxim De Cuyper and Nathan Ngoy bundling the hosts ahead before Jeremy Doku slalomed through the Azzurri defence and confidently shot home. Mark van Bommel's team deservedly claimed a spot in the quarters and made sure the scoreline reflected the balance of play when one of many attacks against an open Italy defence ended with Diego Moreira slotting home with 10 minutes remaining. A dismal night for Italy, who were top of the group after beating France last time out and just needed a draw to go through, was made even worse when Senne Lammens saved Esposito's weak late penalty. top.title: 'Big Noon Kickoff' heading to Ferris State for start of DII playoffs
top.description: The big dogs in college football reside in Big Rapids. And, now, "Big Noon Kickoff" is coming to town. "Big Noon Kickoff," Fox's college football pregame show, has announced that it will broadcast from the campus of Ferris State on Saturday, Nov. 21, for the start of the Division II playoffs. It marks the first trip to a Division II school for "Big Noon Kickoff," and the trip comes after Ferris State set a Division II record with its 41st consecutive victory. Ferris State beat Roosevelt, 63-20, in the regular-season finale Saturday, Nov. 20, to take the all-time record by itself. Ferris State had been tied with rival Grand Valley State with 40 in a row. "I'm so proud of our players and coaches for all the work they have put in to make this happen," Ferris State head coach Tony Annese said Saturday. "This takes a commitment from everyone associated with our program and Bulldog Athletics. It's awesome to see the joy on their faces in a moment like this and the support we've received has been outstanding from everyone." Ferris State football hasn't lost a game since the 2024 playoffs. It has won back-to-back Division II national championships, and this week, it embarks on its quest for a threepeat after an 11-0 regular season. The Bulldogs, led by 20 seniors, are the No. 1 seed in their region, and they open the playoffs against Truman State from Missouri at noon Nov. 21 at Ferris State's Top Taggart Field. And "Big Noon Kickoff" will be there it all. Fox's flagship college football show, which launched in 2019, will broadcast live from campus from 10 a.m. until noon. This will be the third trip to Michigan for "Big Noon Kickoff" this season. It broadcast from Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor twice, for the 17-10 win over Oklahoma on Sept. 12 and the 13-6 overtime loss to Indiana on Oct. 24 . ESPN's "College GameDay," the older rival to the Fox show which debuted in 1994, has never been to a Division II location, though it has broadcast from Football Championship Subdivision schools and one Division III site. The only time either of the shows broadcast in Michigan from a campus other than Michigan or Michigan State was in 2016, when "GameDay" broadcast from Western Michigan on Nov. 19 that year during a season in which the Broncos went undefeated in the regular season, won a Mid-American Conference championship and played in the Cotton Bowl. Fox's "Big Noon Kickoff" broadcast team features analysts Urban Meyer, Mark Ingram II, Matt Leinart and Brady Quinn, host Rob Stone, and reporter Chris Fallica. "I've always said my favorite show locations are places we've either never been or haven't been for a long time," Fallica posted on X (formerly Twitter) after the Ferris State announcement. "This certainly qualifies. "Looking forward to Saturday!" top.description: NEW YORK — Gotham FC did its best to make the most of its relocated semifinal. Unfortunately for the reigning NWSL champions, Kansas City stole the show. nigeria.title: Diabetes: CAPPA urges FG, states to impose 20% sugary drinks tax, reform food policies
nigeria.description: By Chioma Obinna On this day World Diabetes Day, the Corporate Accountability and Public Participation Africa (CAPPA) on Saturday called on the Federal Government and state governments to urgently reform Nigeria’s food policies, impose a minimum 20 per cent tax on sugar-sweetened beverages and tighten regulations on unhealthy food products to curb the rising burden of diabetes. The organisation warned that efforts to tackle the disease would yield limited results if government focused on screening and treatment while allowing aggressive marketing, widespread availability and affordability of ultra-processed foods and sugary drinks to continue unchecked. Making the call in a message to mark the 2026 World Diabetes Day, marked November 14, with the theme, “Early Action on Diabetes”, CAPPA said Nigeria faced an escalating diabetes crisis that required decisive government intervention beyond public awareness and individual lifestyle changes. According to the organisation, Nigeria has the highest number of adults aged 20 to 79 living with diabetes in Africa, while nearly three in four adults with diabetes across the continent remain undiagnosed. It warned that delayed diagnosis exposes millions of Nigerians to potentially life-threatening complications, including kidney failure, blindness, stroke and amputations. CAPPA also raised the alarm over the financial burden of diet-related non-communicable diseases, citing an estimated N1.92 trillion annual out-of-pocket expenditure by Nigerian households on their treatment. Executive Director of CAPPA, Akinbode Oluwafemi, said diabetes prevention should not be reduced to individual discipline when commercial interests and unhealthy food environments increasingly shape people’s dietary choices. He said: “We cannot keep telling Nigerians to eat healthily while allowing unhealthy food and beverages to dominate our markets, schools, advertisements and public spaces. “Early action on diabetes must begin with enacting and implementing strong regulatory policies that make healthy choices possible, affordable and accessible, not simply with advising people to change their dietary behaviour.” The organisation cited its 2025 report, Junk On Our Plates, which documented aggressive marketing of ultra-processed foods and beverages high in sugar and sodium across seven Nigerian states. It said the report exposed the targeting of children, young people and low-income communities through advertising, celebrity endorsements, misleading nutrition labels and cultural imagery designed to promote unhealthy products. To reverse the trend, CAPPA outlined five major policy interventions, beginning with the conclusion and enforcement of the proposed Sugar-Sweetened Beverage (SSB) tax. It urged the House of Representatives and the Federal Executive to complete legislative action following the Senate’s passage of the tax review bill earlier this year. The organisation advocated an inflation-adjusted excise tax of at least 20 per cent

nigeria.title: Igbokoda Crash: NAF recovers black box, holds memorial November 26
nigeria.description: By Kingsley Omonobi The Nigerian Air Force (NAF) has confirmed the recovery of the Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) from the site of the October 5 aircraft crash at Igbokoda, Ondo State, announcing plans to hold a memorial service and wreath-laying ceremony for the victims on November 26. The ceremony will take place at the National Military Cemetery, Abuja, in honour of the personnel and other victims who lost their lives in the NAF 931 aircraft accident. NAF Director of Public Relations and Information, Air Commodore Ehimen Ejodame, disclosed this in a statement on Sunday, saying the event would provide an opportunity for bereaved families, colleagues, friends and members of the Air Force community to pay their last respects. He said the ceremony would also serve as a formal expression of the Service’s respect and remembrance for those who died in the incident. On the recovery of the aircraft’s black box, Ejodame said the CVR, alongside other aircraft fragments and relevant evidence, had been retrieved from the crash site. He explained that data recovered from the voice recorder was being analysed and was expected to contribute significantly to the ongoing investigation into the circumstances surrounding the accident. According to him, the investigation is progressing in collaboration with the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau (NSIB) and the Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA). The Air Force reiterated its commitment to ensuring that the investigation was conducted in accordance with the highest standards of professionalism, transparency, accountability and responsibility, while supporting the independent technical processes required to establish the cause of the crash. The move broke below Friday’s low of about $67,555 and marked the weakest level since mid-August, as weekend trading extended a selloff that has followed a stronger dollar and a fully priced December Federal Reserve rate hike. A week ago, on Nov. 7, bitcoin was trading near $75,750. The decline steepened after Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday, a shake-up that caused AI stocks to sell off which could potentially be responsible for sending bitcoin below $72,000. It slipped toward $71,000 by Thursday evening, then crashed to about $67,555 around midnight Eastern on Friday, its lowest level since August, before recovering toward $69,800 in the morning. The launch introduced the fourth release in the brand’s limited-edition A Night on Earth series, with retail partners Booze.ng, Drinks.ng, Barrels and Naijaliquor and others supporting its presence in the Nigerian market ahead of the festive season. The launch brought the story behind The First Light to life, introducing guests to an expression inspired by the first sunrise of the New Year in New Zealand, one of the first places in the world to welcome the occasion. The release explores the anticipation of new beginnings and the significance of shared moments, themes that resonate with the festive season as people prepare to reconnect with loved ones, celebrate milestones and look ahead to the year to come. Guiding guests through the experience was Yinka Adepetu , The Macallan Brand Educator and Ambassador, who walked them through the inspiration, design and whisky-making craft behind the release. The fourth expression in the series carries its story through a three-layer gift box designed by New Zealand-born artist Bonnie Brown. The artwork captures the transition from dusk to dawn, with crimson bonfires, deep blue fireworks and the amber glow of first light. Together, these elements reflect the atmosphere of New Year celebrations and the anticipation that comes with a fresh start, making the presentation an integral part of the release’s identity. The whisky itself reflects The Macallan’s approach to cask selection and maturation. Matured in sherry-seasoned American and European oak casks, alongside casks that previously held bourbon, the expression presents notes of sweet oak, vanilla, caramelised marshmallows and a hint of Manuka honey on the nose. entertainment.title: Professor Patricia Mamko Lar Makes History as First Female Vice-Chancellor of UNIJOS
entertainment.description: Professor Patricia Mamko Lar, appointed as the 11th substantive Vice-Chancellor and first female Vice-Chancellor of the University of Jos. The University of Jos (UNIJOS) has officially appointed Professor Patricia Mamko Lar as its 11th substantive Vice-Chancellor, making her the first woman to occupy the position since the institution was established in 1971. Announced on Thursday, 12 November 2026 by the university’s Pro-Chancellor and Chairman of Council, Senator Grace Folashade Bent , during a special meeting of the 15th Governing Council, the historic appointment sees Professor Lar succeed Professor Tanko Ishaya as she takes the helm of the Plateau State institution. Born in Langtang, Plateau State, Professor Lar is a distinguished Professor of Medical Microbiology whose career has been deeply woven into the fabric of UNIJOS for nearly four decades. After earning her Bachelor of Science degree in Microbiology from Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria in 1986, she joined the University of Jos in 1987 as a Graduate Assistant in the Department of Medical Microbiology. She later went on to earn her Master’s degree in Medical Microbiology in 1989 and her PhD in Medical Parasitology in 1998 from the University of Lagos, followed by postdoctoral training at the Institute of Human Virology, University of Maryland in the United States under the NIH-Fogarty Fellowship Programme. Rising steadily through the academic ranks, she became an Associate Professor in 2012 before attaining full professorship in October 2015. Over the years, she has built an impressive body of work with more than 40 scholarly publications focusing on infectious diseases, including HIV/AIDS, malaria, antimicrobial resistance, and phytomedicine. Beyond the lecture hall and laboratory, Professor Lar has also served in key administrative roles at UNIJOS—including Head of the Department of Microbiology and Director of Linkages and Collaborations—and previously served a six-month tenure as Acting Vice-Chancellor of Yakubu Gowon University (formerly the University of Abuja) following her appointment by President Bola Tinubu in February 2025. Alongside her academic and leadership credentials, Professor Lar is a recognised advocate for women’s empowerment, having received the He4She Certificate of Award for Women Empowerment Activism in 2019. As she begins her five-year single term as UNIJOS’s first female substantive Vice-Chancellor after 55 years, she brings nearly four decades of institutional experience to the university’s top seat. entertainment.title: Ramla Ali Wins IBF and WBO Titles to Become Somalia’s First Boxing World Champion
entertainment.description: Unified world champion Ramla Ali poses in the ring with her WBO and IBF super-bantamweight belts and her coaching team in Arlington, Texas. Photo Credit: Yahya Ali/Instagram British-Somali boxer and fashion model Ramla Ali is officially a unified world champion! On 8 November 2026 at the College Park Center in Arlington, Texas, the 37-year-old athlete captured the vacant IBF and WBO super-bantamweight world titles after securing a split-decision victory over American contender Mikiah Kreps . During the ten-round bout, Ali dropped Kreps with a sharp right hand in the third round—the sole knockdown of the night—before two judges scored the contest 97–92 and 96–93 in her favour, against one scorecard of 98–91 for Kreps. With this triumph, Ali became Somalia’s first-ever professional boxing world champion and a unified titleholder in one unforgettable night. Born in Mogadishu, Somalia, she fled the civil war as a child with her family and grew up in East London, initially taking up boxing in secret as a teenager before turning it into a life-changing calling. Ramla Ali makes her ring walk behind the Somali and British flags ahead of her super-bantamweight world title fight in Arlington, Texas. Photo Credit: Yahya Ali/Instagram Her remarkable journey from refugee to Olympic athlete and champion is also the subject of the biographical feature film In the Shadows. Directed by Anthony Wonke , the film premiered at the 70th BFI London Film Festival on 9 October 2026 before opening in UK and Irish cinemas on 30 October—just over a week before she lifted her world title belts in Texas. BAFTA-winning Top Boy actress Jasmine Jobson stars as Ali alongside Peaky Blinders actor Finn Cole as her husband and former coach, Richard Moore , with both Ali and Moore serving as executive producers on the project. This championship milestone builds on a string of barrier-breaking firsts across sports, cinema, and fashion. Long before her title win in Arlington, Ali made history as the first Muslim woman to win an English amateur boxing title, the first boxer to win an international gold medal while representing Somalia, and the first boxer to represent Somalia on the Olympic stage when she competed in the women’s featherweight division at the Tokyo 2020 Summer Olympics. Ramla Ali celebrates in the ring as the referee raises her hand following her split-decision victory over Mikiah Kreps on 8 November 2026. Photo Credit: Yahya Ali/Instagram Away from the ring, she has carved out an equally notable space in global luxury fashion. Ali has graced the covers of British Vogue, Elle UK, Harper’s Bazaar Arabia, and Grazia UK, served as a brand ambassador for Cartier and Dior, and made history as the first boxer to wear custom ring attire created by major fashion houses—including bespoke fight kits designed by Dior, Off-White, Versace, Alexander McQueen, and Burberry featuring the panther emblem from Somalia’s coat of arms. There is a lot that goes into establishing a successful business. It requires developing the business idea, securing clients, building a customer base and eventually bringing people on board. Starting a business and watching it grow can be an exciting experience. However, one thing many start-up founders overlook is the importance of having the right organisational structure in place. It is one thing to have a great business idea and attract talented employees, but it is another thing to create an environment where everyone understands their responsibilities, knows who they report to and can work effectively towards achieving the company’s objectives. I once worked with a client who needed a new set of employees for a business establishment that was reopening after a period of restructuring. As part of the recruitment process, the first thing I ensured was that a manager was hired before proceeding to fill the remaining vacancies. The idea was simple. The manager would oversee the day-to-day running of the establishment, ensure that company policies were implemented and periodically train employees based on the requirements of their respective roles. During the recruitment process, I clearly communicated each employee’s responsibilities and the person they would be reporting to. These details were also stated in their respective offer letters, so everyone understood their roles and the management structure they were expected to work within. However, there was a challenge. Before the manager was hired, an accountant who was personally known to both co-founders had also been in charge of the previous employees. Following the restructuring, the founders had communicated their desire for a new operational arrangement, and this was clearly reflected in the recruitment brief. Although the new employees understood that they were expected to report to the newly hired manager, the existing employees still had their loyalty to the accountant, who had previously been in charge. The challenge was that the new management structure had not been properly implemented within the organisation. entertainment.title: Uwaezu Kanu: Why Motherhood Feels Different for Women in Their 40s Today
entertainment.description: “Oh my God, Uwaezu! You need to hear the latest gist!” My younger sister buzzed with excitement. Though we had been living in different countries for a couple of years, we still made time to talk every single week. Unfortunately, when she called, I couldn’t talk on the phone as I had been ambushed by my kids, who were brandishing their homework and threatening to cry if I didn’t help them. As a mom herself, she immediately understood why I couldn’t continue with the conversation. I quickly made my excuses, and we laughed and hung up, promising to catch up at a more convenient time. However, that exchange got me thinking about how most millennial women have a radically different marriage and motherhood timeline from our mothers. You see, when my mother was in her early 40s, my siblings and I were in university, so she had a lot of free time during the week to spend relaxing, hanging out with her friends, and attending social events. Basically living her best life. I, on the other hand, at 40-plus, spend my days cooking pot after pot of hot meals that immediately get devoured by my ever-hungry kids, teaching my nursery school-aged kids how to count and spell, and trying but often failing to enforce a strict bedtime with yelling and threats. I constantly feel myself going underwater and have to fight for my life every single day. There are other ways motherhood has been such a hugely different experience for me than it was for my mother. Like many women of her generation, she got married right after secondary school as university education was not seen as vital. This meant that she was a teenage mother and so had more energy to spare on her kids. She also benefited from having a lot of support from domestic staff and relatives. I do not have any village supporting me with child-rearing. I have hired domestic staff in the past, but it was always one thing or another, and they ended up leaving me stranded. I also do not have youth on my side, and I have the back pain and other aches to prove it. But this experience is not unique to me. Statistics show that most women globally will have their first child at 30 or 31, and we are seeing a lot more women becoming first-time moms at 35 and above. This is considered advanced maternal age. The fact is that as women increasingly prioritise university education and career stability before marriage, maternal age will continue to rise. This is not a trend that can be reversed. sports.title: 'Couldn't get worse': Klopp calls for change in FIFA leadership
sports.description: Germany coach Jurgen Klopp has called for a change in FIFA leadership. (Pedja Milosavljevic) Germany coach Jurgen Klopp called on Sunday for an end to Gianni Infantino's time as FIFA president, saying he "did not think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter." Speaking in Berlin ahead of Monday's Nations League clash with the Netherlands, Klopp said the next candidate for football's global governing body should have the game's interests at heart. "I've been following football for many years. There are people who are much more knowledgeable about this than I am. But I think most people now agree a change would make a lot of sense," Klopp said. "I didn't think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that." President of FIFA from 1998, Blatter resigned in disgrace in 2015 amid corruption allegations, including accusations he had sought to buy votes for his presidency. Charges were brought against Blatter who was eventually cleared in two trials, but was banned from football by FIFA's ethics committee. Klopp added: "Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job." Swiss Infantino succeeded Blatter as FIFA president in 2016 and has come under heavy criticism for a series of decisions and proposals, including his plan to sell off part of the commercial rights of the World Cup and creating a 'Peace Prize' award for US President Donald Trump. "There are people who truly care about the future of football -- people who aren't driven by financial interests," said Klopp. "If someone like that were to step up -- if someone like that were to become president -- I think that would be a significant improvement." "There are surely people who care deeply about the future of football and have no financial interests in it." The next election for FIFA president takes place in March 2027. Only former Swiss footballer Ramon Vega and Japan's Kozo Tashima have announced their intention to run against Infantino although Arsene Wenger has also been mentioned. Klopp did not discuss the other candidates, but said: "I've heard something about Arsene Wenger. Not sure if that's true or false, but he's a good man." dwi/td/pb

sports.description: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The goalie depth chart in the New York Rangers organization received yet another minor reshuffling Sunday, when they acquired Arvid Soderblom from the Chicago Blackhawks in exchange for Spencer Martin . Soderblom will swap places with Martin on the Hartford Wolf Pack roster in the American Hockey League. New York had little faith in Martin, who’s 31 and didn’t exactly excel in the NHL last season when Igor Shesterkin landed on IR for a month with a lower-body injury in January. sports.title: 'Big Noon Kickoff' heading to Ferris State for start of DII playoffs
sports.description: The big dogs in college football reside in Big Rapids. And, now, "Big Noon Kickoff" is coming to town. "Big Noon Kickoff," Fox's college football pregame show, has announced that it will broadcast from the campus of Ferris State on Saturday, Nov. 21, for the start of the Division II playoffs. It marks the first trip to a Division II school for "Big Noon Kickoff," and the trip comes after Ferris State set a Division II record with its 41st consecutive victory. Ferris State beat Roosevelt, 63-20, in the regular-season finale Saturday, Nov. 20, to take the all-time record by itself. Ferris State had been tied with rival Grand Valley State with 40 in a row. "I'm so proud of our players and coaches for all the work they have put in to make this happen," Ferris State head coach Tony Annese said Saturday. "This takes a commitment from everyone associated with our program and Bulldog Athletics. It's awesome to see the joy on their faces in a moment like this and the support we've received has been outstanding from everyone." Ferris State football hasn't lost a game since the 2024 playoffs. It has won back-to-back Division II national championships, and this week, it embarks on its quest for a threepeat after an 11-0 regular season. The Bulldogs, led by 20 seniors, are the No. 1 seed in their region, and they open the playoffs against Truman State from Missouri at noon Nov. 21 at Ferris State's Top Taggart Field. And "Big Noon Kickoff" will be there it all. Fox's flagship college football show, which launched in 2019, will broadcast live from campus from 10 a.m. until noon. This will be the third trip to Michigan for "Big Noon Kickoff" this season. It broadcast from Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor twice, for the 17-10 win over Oklahoma on Sept. 12 and the 13-6 overtime loss to Indiana on Oct. 24 . ESPN's "College GameDay," the older rival to the Fox show which debuted in 1994, has never been to a Division II location, though it has broadcast from Football Championship Subdivision schools and one Division III site. The only time either of the shows broadcast in Michigan from a campus other than Michigan or Michigan State was in 2016, when "GameDay" broadcast from Western Michigan on Nov. 19 that year during a season in which the Broncos went undefeated in the regular season, won a Mid-American Conference championship and played in the Cotton Bowl. Fox's "Big Noon Kickoff" broadcast team features analysts Urban Meyer, Mark Ingram II, Matt Leinart and Brady Quinn, host Rob Stone, and reporter Chris Fallica. sports.description: BOSTON — NBA games are rarely decided in the first quarter, however, a Sunday afternoon showdown between the Boston Celtics and the Dallas Mavericks might be an exception. Boston blitzed Dallas in the first frame, outscoring its Western Conference opponent 42-9 to open the 131-94 victory at TD Garden. The Celtics gave up just 2 field goals through 12 minutes of play, which is the lowest amount of made shots they've ever allowed in the first quarter of a game in franchise history. Boston continued to impress from there, as it held a 67-37 lead heading into halftime after shooting a blistering 50 percent from the field. Although the C's got production from almost every one of their players, star forward Jayson Tatum led the way with a game-high 32 points. He also recorded 6 rebounds and 6 assists in 30 minutes of action. Meanwhile, the Mavericks were nowhere near as productive. They were on the second night of a back-to-back and missed the presence of star point guard Kyrie Irving, who was sidelined due to injury management. Star forward Cooper Flag notched 17 points in his second game ever in Boston — just 3 hours away from his hometown of Newport, Maine. Flagg had a homecoming to forget, though, tallying 3 turnovers in 27 minutes and missing 10 of his 15 shots from the floor. Following the 37-point blowout, the Celtics are 11-2 on the season and remain in first place in the Eastern Conference. sports.description: A day after Ferris State football set the NCAA Division II record with its 41 st consecutive victory, the school reportedly got another historic win. Fox’s “Big Noon Saturday” is reportedly headed to Big Rapids for its morning kickoff show on Saturday, Nov. 21, ahead of the Bulldogs opening the Division II playoffs at Top Taggart Field at 1 p.m. against Truman State. The news was first reported by Brett McMurphy of On3 . MAKING HISTORY: Ferris State makes NCAA history with record 41st straight win It’s the first time in its eight seasons that the pregame show, featuring Rob Stone, Urban Meyer, Matt Leinart, Brady Quinn and Mark Ingram II, has spent a Saturday on a D-II campus. ESPN’s move venerated show, “College GameDay,” has also never broadcast from a D-II campus. The Bulldogs received a 1-seed in their region in the 32-team field as they go for their fifth national title in six years, as well as attempting to become just the second program with three straight D-II titles (North Alabama, 1993-95). A win over Truman would send the Bulldogs into the second round to face either Findlay (Ohio) or Augustana (South Dakota). On the other side of Ferris’ region, however, wait a trio of Michigan rivals: Grand Valley State faces 2-seed Northwood in Midland at 1 p.m. Saturday; the winner of that game faces the winner between Minnesota State and Michigan Tech, with the game to be played in Houghton at 1 p.m. Saturday. The Huskies are making just their third NCAA Tournament appearance, and first since 2014. Ferris, meanwhile, is making its 12 th consecutive NCAA appearance. Ferris State last lost in its 2024 season opener, to Pittsburg State (of Kansas) on Aug. 31, 2024. The next week, the Bulldogs wiped out Lake Erie, 56-3, to start its record run. The 799-day streak has included 20 GLIAC wins as well as nine NCAA playoff victories, including title game wins over Valdosta State in 2024 and Harding in 2025. The Bulldogs, coached by Tony Annese, are coming off a pair of GLIAC-clinching wins (against Wayne State in Detroit and Roosevelt) by a combined score of 143-20. Saturday’s victory in Big Rapids snapped a tie with Grand Valley State for the D-II record and also moved Ferris State into second for the longest streak among Division I (FBS- or FCS-level) and Division II programs, passing Washington’s 40-game run from 1908-14 and GVSU’s 40-game run from 2005-07. Oklahoma, at 47 wins from 1953-57, is the FBS-level record holder, while North Dakota State owns the FCS-level mark at 39 wins from 2017-20. The longest streak in NCAA football, however, belongs to Division III Mount Union, which won 55 straight from 2000-03. Another title for Ferris State – with the D-II championship game set for McKinney, Texas, on Dec. 19 – would mean five wins, putting the Bulldogs just three wins next season from passing the Sooners for the second-longest NCAA streak. A bunch of aliens known as the Nerdlucks arrive on Earth to abduct the Tunes and take them back as attractions to the outer-space amusement park known as Moron Mountain (shockingly nobody has claimed that subreddit, so do your thing, Internet!). So, Bugs and friends reach out to Michael Jordan, who recently switched from basketball to baseball, to help the Tune Squad win this intergalactic b-ball matchup and their freedom, because if anybody can do it, Air Jordan (Hare Jordan?) can. Oh, Bill Murray also shows up here a few times. Why? Because he can! (Image credit: Warner Bros. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
science.description: null On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) Why it mattered When the 300-foot telescope first debuted, it was not just the United States' largest radio observatory, but the largest such facility in the world. But its quick construction — just two years — led to it having to be significantly upgraded later. "In 1970, the 300-foot’s surface had become so warped from maintenance crews, snow, and its own weight that a new finer-meshed aluminum surface was installed," the website for the National Radio Astronomy Observatory reads. "A larger traveling feed was also installed at the prime focus." The collapse, however, was no one's fault. "Unforeseeable stress factors cracked a steel connector plate," wrote the NRAO. The Green Bank Telescope collapse left a mass of twisted debris behind. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) During its years of observations, the 300-foot telescope contirbuted to the discovery of dark matter and the realization that pulsars come from supernova explosions. "One of the most important products to come out of the 300-foot telescope was an all-sky survey of radio objects called the Green Bank 6cm Survey. Nearly every northern hemisphere radio object studied by any other telescope is from a catalog compiled using this telescope," reads the NRAO website. Want more space history? science.description: null For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold. Next comes a dramatic nova explosion that causes the star to flare to 1,000 times its usual brightness before gradually settling down and repeating the cycle. Why is it so challenging to predict T. CrB's nova flare? "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email. "Everyone is very confident on this. But we cannot make high-accuracy measures of the rate of gas falling onto the surface of the white dwarf, and we do not have a high accuracy measure of the trigger mass for the big hydrogen bomb." Schaefer continued. Historical observations reveal that the last nova eruption reached Earth in 1946, which places us well inside the window for another dramatic brightening of T. CrBb. However, the unpredictability of the white dwarf's feeding makes it difficult to pin down exactly when the explosion will become visible from Earth. An animation of T. CrB brightening. (Image credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab) "The exact date of the upcoming T CrB eruption depends primarily on how fast the gas coming from its companion star is accumulating on the surface of the white dwarf," explained Schaefer. "When some specific trigger mass has accumulated, then T CrB will erupt. For the last 80 years, we have been watching the gas pile up on the white dwarf surface, and we know that it must be near the trigger threshold." I can't give you a guaranteed prediction, but I will be a little surprised if it gets to 2030, or 84 years past the last eruption." science.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
science.description: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year. On June 14, as it headed towards perihelion – the closest point in its orbit to the sun, at a distance from our star of 1.5 times the distance between the Earth and the sun (known as an astronomical unit) , 220P suddenly and without warning burst into life. On 31 May, the comet was languishing at magnitude +17.39 (the higher the magnitude, the fainter an object is), but within less than 14 hours it had dramatically brightened to magnitude +11.05, bringing it into range for observation with small amateur telescopes. By June 2, 220P was up to magnitude +8.23 and was technically visible for a short while in 10x50 binoculars from a dark site, prompting amateur astronomers and astrophotographers to chase down this rare event. By perihelion, the comet had faded back to magnitude +12, but more was to come. A second outburst began at the end of July, brightening from magnitude +14 on 28 July to magnitude 6.1 by 6 August. Telling the tale of a dirty snowball Comets are often referred to as dirty snowballs, and beneath their dusty crust are ices made from various volatiles, including water, carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Solar heating, even at the distance of Mars, can cause these ices to rapidly sublimate into gases, and the pressure of the escaping gas rips the surface apart, spewing huge amounts of dust in to space. Models based on observations of 220P’s outburst indicate that it spewed out between tens of billions and hundreds of billions of pounds’ worth of cometary dust that filled the comet’s coma, the diffuse 'atmosphere' that clings to the comet’s solid nucleus. The dust particles, which are just millionths of a meter across, expanded outwards from the comet at about 1,280 feet (390 meters) per second, scattering sunlight and causing the coma to substantially brighten. "We have concluded that the comet detached localized parts of its crust, creating a dust-rich envelope that increased [the comet’s brightness by] 250 times in half a day," Josep M. Trigo-Rodríguez, of the Institut de Ciències de l’Espai and the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia in Spain, said in a statement . science.title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?
science.description: null Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running. The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully , nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off. Long-distance view of Ship's historic landing on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) SpaceX has caught Super Heavy on three test flights to date. But it had never caught a Ship before; indeed, it had never even tried before Saturday. It's tougher and riskier to catch Ship; the upper stage flies much higher and faster than Super Heavy, so its return trip is much more more involved. Saturday was therefore a very big day for the company. "That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes." The F light 15 mission plan gave us a sneak peek at the future: The double catch will be standard on operational Starship missions, as this recovery strategy will enable rapid inspection, refurbishment and reflight of the megarocket, according to SpaceX. And the company is indeed planning on rapid reflight. Elon Musk has said that SpaceX is targeting 10,000 Starship launches per year by 2030, which works out to more than one liftoff every hour on average. Why such a mind-boggling cadence? Because SpaceX plans to build megaconstellations far larger than anything circling Earth today. For example, it wants its next-gen Starlink V3 broadband network to consist of 100,000 satellites . And its planned Starmind AI data-center constellation will be 10 times bigger than that, featuring one million spacecraft , if all goes to plan. For perspective: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network in low Earth orbit (LEO), by far the largest constellation ever assembled, is about 11,000 strong at the moment. A look at the 33 Raptor engines of Starship's Super Heavy booster during the vehicle's Flight 15 test launch on Nov. 14, 2026. science.title: 'Alien: Fireteam Elite 2' is a good old-fashioned bug hunt, ironically plagued by bugs
science.description: The first Aliens: Fireteam Elite was among my favorite Alien video games , and there were a lot of reasons to be excited for a sequel. At Summer Game Fest 2026 , we learned of many smart changes and improvements to the formula, and I was eager to go bug-hunting again. A new campaign, fully reworked classes, and four-player co-op. What could go wrong? Months later, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2's debut has been difficult, mostly due to glaring tech issues. Despite this, it's still a welcome jolt of action for a franchise that's been focusing on making the Xenomorphs scary again in recent years. Alien: Romulus (2024) and Alien: Earth (2025) have reestablished the acid-blooded Xenomorphs as bona fide horror icons, while games like Aliens: Dark Descent bet on tense real-time tactics and squad management; Rogue Incursion spooked VR and non-VR players alike; and we even have Isolation 2 's pure survival horror to look forward to. Rough edges aside, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is a necessary return to mindless shooting and treating the Xenos as a relentless horde, dropping the stalking and slasher-inspired murders in favor of sci-fi shootouts and macho one-liners. It's far from a novel idea — even the original game is only five years old — but a classic for a reason. Another glorious day in the Corps (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) Believe it or not, another colony has fallen prey to the Xenomorphs in Fireteam Elite 2. The familiar setup takes a new team of Colonial Marines to a mining facility on LV-558, where contact has been lost with the first wave of Marines that went in to deal with the threat. This isn't first contact; the Marines are more than used to bug hunts by now, which means there's less exposition to cut through before getting to the Xeno-blasting chaos. The writing certainly won't stun the Academy (and there's definitely too much of it in between missions), but the agility here is appreciated. We've fought these aliens many, many times before. Fireteam Elite 2 is smart enough to sidestep fake tension and just hit the ground running. (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) All the design changes and upgrades reinforce the intent to make the ultimate Aliens action game. Classes have more defined roles and access to better, more destructive sci-fi weapons, and the upgrade to four-player fireteams is welcome when aliens and hostile synths won't stop pouring in. Tired of replaying campaign missions on higher difficulties and with modifiers? Prepare for the worst in this shooter's version of the classic horde mode. At its best, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 understands why James Cameron's masterpiece still holds up. During the biggest Xenomorph onslaughts — when the bullets are flying and acid is spraying — the game's shortcomings and jankier elements fade away. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
science.description: null On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier. The Apollo 12 moonwalkers also performed a lot of moon science. The astronauts picked up 75 pounds of moon rocks. Most of the rocks were basalts that formed from molten lava. These basalts showed the Apollo 12 landing site is more than 3 billion years old. The Apollo 12 astronauts on NASA's second crewed moon landing mission. They are (left to right) are Charles Conrad Jr., Richard F. Gordon Jr., and Alan L. Bean. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered Apollo 12 proved that the Apollo 11 moon landing was not just a one-off stunt while setting the stage for even more ambitious missions. To truly explore the moon and advance our understanding of how our solar system formed, the follow-on Apollo flights needed to be able to land where the geologists had identified as areas of interest. Apollo 12, with its touchdown in proximity to the Surveyor probe, proved this was possible. The Apollo 12 astronauts visited NASA's Surveyor 3 lander and took samples of it back to Earth. (Image credit: NASA) The launch of Apollo 12 also underscored the importance of having a well-prepared Mission Control team, an asset that would be critical to outcome of the next mission, Apollo 13. The ability to recover from a complete electrical short out with the simple call of a through of a switch "SCE to AUX" proved that knowing every detail about how the spacecraft worked was key to a successful program. science.title: 'Now everything changes': SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for 1st time ever (video)
science.description: null SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential. Starship launched on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov. 13), rising into the sky from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. The mission plan called for bringing both of the vehicle's stages back to Starbase and catching them with the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — an unprecedented total recovery of an orbital rocket . That didn't happen; Starship's Super Heavy booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship succeeded in its attempt, notching a huge milestone for SpaceX and its dream of full rocket reuse. "That was the missing link," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast today, his voice thick with emotion. "That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes." SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Space.com) The Ship catch occurred today at 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT; 3:20 p.m. local Texas time), roughly 22.5 hours after Flight 15 lifted off. Many SpaceX employees went outside to watch the vehicle, known as Ship 42, descend through the clouds toward its Starbase launch tower, which the company calls "Mechazilla." And they got quite a show: Ship 42 nestled gently into Mechazilla's waiting arms, while "Baby Come Back" played over SpaceX's landing webcast. "This is so incredible to see," SpaceX's Jessie Anderson said during the livestream. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes." Why was this such a big deal? SpaceX had already caught Super Heavy — on three previous Starship test flights, in fact. But it had never tried before with Ship. The upper stage is a tougher target, for it flies higher, farther and faster than the booster. Indeed, on Flight 15, Ship 42 came all the way back down from orbit. Ship 42 comes in for its landing on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) While the double-catch attempt, and the chopsticks success with Ship, were Flight 15's main headlines, the mission had other objectives as well. One was getting Ship to orbit, which had happened on just one previous Starship launch — Flight 14 , which lifted off on Sept. 28. science.title: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
science.description: null Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029. Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky . It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth . The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years , when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse. Jupiter, Mars and Regulus will appear close together on the night of Nov. 15-16. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva.) Both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus , which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun . A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant , formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams. How to measure distances in the night sky using your outstretched hand. (Image credit: Created in Canva Pro) Mars, meanwhile, appears as a reddish, ochre disk complete with dark surface features, where basaltic rock has been scoured clean of the iron-rich dust that covers much of its surface, according to NASA . science.title: New Scientist readers on how the magazine has shaped their lives
science.description: Have you been reading New Scientist since the start? Getty Images/Westend61 The first issue of New Scientist was published on 22 November 1956, and some of our readers have been with us since the very beginning. We asked subscribers, young and old, to tell us how they first encountered the magazine and how New Scientist has influenced their lives. The volume of responses and the gratitude expressed within them were quite overwhelming. Here are some of our favourites, featuring a spectacular maggot experiment, science-inspired poetry and even a match made on the short-lived New Scientist dating site. Huge thanks to everyone who wrote in. I was interested to see that New Scientist was launched “for all those men and women who are interested in scientific discovery and in its industrial, commercial and social consequences”. At the age of 13, I saved up a shilling from my Saturday morning “jobs” to purchase the first edition on 22 November 1956 and became one of those people interested in scientific discovery. Seventy years later, I remain a subscriber, after a scientific career that took me to many (if not, most!) countries in the world. New Scientist covered things like the opening of Jodrell Bank telescope in 1957. Since that was only about 50 miles (80 kilometres) away, it necessitated a bike ride to see what it really looked like! Peter Hall Advertisement I seem to have been reading New Scientist for the full 70! I do recall my encounter with the first edition: I was at Bec Grammar School in south London in a second-year physics class – it was 1956. The teacher, a genial boffin-type, announced the advent of the new publication and handed out copies – all I remember is its grey (or was it beige?) pages, which I read in a perfunctory way (I was only 12!) little thinking it would follow me through life and around the globe. Robyn Williams I was at Malvern College in England for my O level examinations from 1955 to 1958. My science master at Malvern had recognised my interest in science and technology and he bought the very first issue of New Scientist with his own money. At the next science class, he stood up in front of the whole class and waved the first issue, saying, “Young Inman, a new UK science and technology magazine has been published and here is the first issue for you.” I went on to reach 60 years as a member of the UK Institution of Civil Engineers. Peter Inman 1956 puts me back at school – Fettes College in Edinburgh. The school adopted New Scientist from its first edition and it was available in the library, where senior boys interested in science were recommended to read it. And so began a lifetime of New Scientist – I have been a regular for as long as I can remember and a subscriber for a very long time. I am very grateful to New Scientist for maintaining my interest in all the sciences and new developments, which I am sure has helped me to think laterally and to have a greater understanding of what makes everything tick. science.title: SpaceX launches Starship on ambitious 22-hour Flight 15 test, but aborts booster 'chopsticks' catch (video)
science.description: null STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX launched the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX 's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. The flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch. Following stage separation, Super Heavy reoriented for a planned return to Starbase as Ship powered its way toward low Earth orbit (LEO). SpaceX originally planned to catch Super Heavy with the Starbase launch tower's giant mechanical "chopstick" arms. But it wasn't to be: The company called off the catch attempt and brought the booster down for a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after launch, for reasons that were not immediately clear. A successful catch would have been a significant milestone for SpaceX and its efforts to design Starship as a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle. It would have been the first successful recovery of a Version 3 (V3) Super Heavy , which SpaceX began flying earlier this year. The company previously recovered three of its V1 Super Heavy vehicles and reused two of those in later flights. SpaceX's Starship megarocket launches on its 15th test flight from Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Future/Josh Dinner, Space.com) Ship goes to orbit Ship's Raptors continued to fire following stage separation, completing their first burn just after eight minutes into flight. All went according to plan after that for Ship as well: A second engine burn lasting about 20 seconds parked Ship in LEO at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) at T+26 minutes and 10 seconds. "We’ve got a nominal orbit insertion, so Starship now in orbit around Earth for the second time ever," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during today's Flight 15 launch webcast. "That’s a really great moment." Ship first reached orbit on Flight 14 , which launched on Sept. 28. Ship carried 26 of SpaceX's Starlink V3 spacecraft, which were deployed into LEO on schedule today over a 42-minute span starting 35 minutes after launch. The upgraded wireless internet satellites are the second V3 batch to reach orbit, after a set of 26 that were delivered on Flight 14 . V3s are significantly more powerful than SpaceX's V2 Starlinks, which currently number more than 11,000 in LEO. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
science.description: null On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. When Mariner 9 got to Mars , it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona. Mariner 9 worked for one year in orbit. When it ran out of gas, NASA shut it off. But the spacecraft remains one of the most famous Mars voyagers of all time. The Mariner 9 spacecraft, seen here in a NASA model, was the first to orbit Mars in 1971. (Image credit: NASA) Here's why it mattered Mariner 9 cemented its place in space history when it entered into orbit around Mars, the first human-built spacecraft ever to do so. The NASA spacecraft actually beat the Soviet Union's own Mars 2 spacecraft to the Red Planet, even though Mars 2 "had an 11-day head start," NASA said in a mission description . (Mars 2 would go on to be the first human-built craft to impact the surface of Mars when it crashed into the Red Planet.) But it was the science from Mariner 9 that transformed Mars from a mysterious Red Planet into a full world for humans to explore. The Boldest Mars Missions in History The Mariner 9 mission first saw the peak of Olympus Mons on Mars in the midst of a global dust storm in 1971. (Image credit: NASA/JPL) Mariner 9 carried four primary instruments to study Mars, including a camera system for imaging, an ultraviolet spectrometer, an infrared spectrometer and an infrared radiometer. The probe mapped 85% of Mars with those tools during its nearly one-year mission. The Mariner 9 spacecraft discovered 20 giant volcanoes on Mars (including Olympus Mars) and made key observations to map Valles Marineris, which runs 2,500 miles (4,000 kilometers) long acros the Tharsis region and is 120 miles (200 km) wide. "The canyon was named in honor of Mariner 9," NASA said in an overview . In all, Mariner 9 took 7,329 photos of the surface of Mars, mapping the planet down to a resolution of between 1/2-1 mile (1-2 km). It also snapped at least 80 photos of Phobos and Deimos, the two small moons of Mars. By February 1972, Mariner 9's supply of gaseous nitrogen, which it used to feed its attitide control thrusters, had run dry. NASA finally shut down the mission in October 1972.
